```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)

set.seed(258)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

plot_cols <- list(
  teal        = "#00695c",
  teal_dark   = "#004d40",
  teal_light  = "#e0f2f1",
  blue        = "#c8e6f3",
  blue_soft   = "#eef8fb",
  grey        = "#f5f6f7",
  yellow      = "#fff8e1",
  orange      = "#f9a825",
  red         = "#c62828",
  text        = "#2f3437",
  muted       = "#667174",
  border      = "#d8dee2",
  code        = "#f3f4f5",
  white       = "#ffffff"
)

plotly_anova_layout <- function(
  p,
  title = NULL,
  x_title = NULL,
  y_title = NULL,
  height = 360,
  margin = list(l = 70, r = 24, t = 58, b = 64)
) {
  p |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, font = list(size = 16), x = 0.02),
      height = height,
      margin = margin,
      xaxis = list(
        title = x_title,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        fixedrange = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      yaxis = list(
        title = y_title,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        fixedrange = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      dragmode = FALSE,
      paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
      plot_bgcolor = "white",
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    config(
      displayModeBar = FALSE,
      displaylogo = FALSE,
      scrollZoom = FALSE,
      doubleClick = FALSE,
      responsive = FALSE
    )
}
```

function resizePlotlyOnSlides() {

  document.querySelectorAll(".js-plotly-plot").forEach(function(plot) {
    Plotly.Plots.resize(plot);
  });
}
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {

  setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 750);
  setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 1500);
  if (window.Reveal) {
    Reveal.on("ready", function () { setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 300); });
    Reveal.on("slidechanged", function () { setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 300); });
    Reveal.on("fragmentshown", function () { setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 300); });
    Reveal.on("fragmenthidden", function () { setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 300); });
  }
  window.addEventListener("resize", resizePlotlyOnSlides);
});
</script>

## Chapter Roadmap {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.1 - ANOVA model</span>
Compare $k \ge 3$ population means using one global model.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.2 - Variation split</span>
Break total variation into treatment variation and error variation.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.3 - ANOVA F test</span>
Use the ANOVA table and a right-tailed $F$ distribution.
:::
::::

<br>

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.4 - Assumptions</span>
Normal residuals, equal population variance, and independent observations.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.5 - Pairwise comparisons</span>
After rejecting ANOVA, compare means in pairs.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.6 - R checks</span>
Use `aov()`, `anova(lm())`, and `pairwise.t.test()` to check ANOVA and pairwise comparisons.
:::
::::


---

## Why ANOVA? {.compact .why-anova}

:::: {.why-anova-flow style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto auto auto; gap: 14px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.defbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.66em; line-height: 1.17; padding: 16px 20px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Purpose</span>

**Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)** is used to compare several population means at once.

Instead of running many separate two-sample tests, ANOVA begins with one **global test**.
:::

:::: {.three-col style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.95fr 1.05fr 1.05fr; gap: 16px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 16px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Question</span>

Do all groups have the same population mean?

$$
k \ge 3
$$

groups are being compared.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 16px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Null hypothesis</span>

The population means are all equal:

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
$$
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 16px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Alternative hypothesis</span>

At least one population mean is different:

$$
H_a:\text{not all }\mu_i\text{ are equal}
$$
:::

::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.65em; line-height: 1.17; padding: 15px 20px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Key idea</span>

ANOVA tells us whether there is evidence that **at least one mean differs**.

If ANOVA rejects \(H_0\), then pairwise comparisons can ask **which means differ**.
:::

::::

---

## One-Factor ANOVA Model {.compact .anova-model}

:::: {.anova-model-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 16px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.defbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 15px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Textbook model</span>

For observation $j$ in group $i$:

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
$$

Here, $Y_{ij}$ is the response value for observation $j$ in group $i$.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 15px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Equivalent form</span>

Since the population mean for group $i$ is

$$
\mu_i=\mu+\tau_i,
$$

the same model can be written as

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
$$
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 16px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Meaning of the notation</span>

- $\mu$: overall population mean
- $\tau_i$: treatment effect for group $i$
- $\epsilon_{ij}$: random error for observation $j$ in group $i$
- $\mu_i=\mu+\tau_i$: population mean of group $i$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 16px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Intuition</span>

Each observation is modeled as

$$
\text{response}
=
\text{group mean}
+
\text{random error}.
$$

So ANOVA asks whether all group means are equal:

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
$$

or whether at least one group mean differs.
:::

::::

---

## Data Structure and Notation {.compact .data-notation}

:::: {.data-notation-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.52fr 0.48fr; gap: 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.col style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 14px;"}

::: {.stat-card style="font-size: 0.50em; line-height: 1.04; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Data layout</span>

| Group 1 | Group 2 | $\cdots$ | Group $k$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $X_{11}$ | $X_{21}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{k1}$ |
| $X_{12}$ | $X_{22}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{k2}$ |
| $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\ddots$ | $\vdots$ |
| $X_{1n_1}$ | $X_{2n_2}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{kn_k}$ |
| $\bar X_1$ | $\bar X_2$ | $\cdots$ | $\bar X_k$ |
| $S_1^2$ | $S_2^2$ | $\cdots$ | $S_k^2$ |
| $n_1$ | $n_2$ | $\cdots$ | $n_k$ |
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 15px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Notation</span>

- $\bar X_i$: sample mean of group $i$
- $S_i^2$: sample variance of group $i$
- $n_i$: sample size of group $i$
:::

:::

::: {.defbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 15px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Overall summaries</span>

Total sample size:

$$
n=n_1+n_2+\cdots+n_k
$$

Overall sample mean:

$$
\bar X
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}X_{ij}
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_i\bar X_i
$$
:::

::::

---

## ANOVA as a Prediction Problem {.compact .anova-prediction}

:::: {.prediction-flow style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto auto auto; gap: 10px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.defbox style="font-size: 0.60em; line-height: 1.12; padding: 12px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Main idea</span>

ANOVA compares **two prediction rules**: one that ignores the group and one that uses the group.
:::

:::: {.two-col style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 14px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.54em; line-height: 1.06; padding: 13px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Ignore group information</span>

Predict every observation using the overall mean:

$$
\widehat X_{ij}=\bar X
$$

Total prediction error:

$$
SSTotal=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(X_{ij}-\bar X)^2
$$

All observations are treated as coming from one common center.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.54em; line-height: 1.06; padding: 13px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Use group information</span>

Predict observation $j$ in group $i$ using its group mean:

$$
\widehat X_{ij}=\bar X_i
$$

Remaining prediction error:

$$
SSE=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(X_{ij}-\bar X_i)^2
$$

Each group is allowed to have its own center.
:::

::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 12px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Improvement from using groups</span>

The variation explained by group membership is the reduction in prediction error:

$$
SSTr=SSTotal-SSE
$$

If this improvement is large compared with the within-group error, the ANOVA \(F\) statistic becomes large.
:::

::::

---

## Sources of Variation

::: {.defbox}
ANOVA works by splitting variation into two pieces: variation **within** groups and variation **between** groups.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Within groups: error variation</span>

$$
SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(n_i-1)S_i^2
$$

This is residual variation inside the groups.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Between groups: treatment variation</span>

$$
SSTr=\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i(\bar X_i-\bar X)^2
$$

This captures how group means differ from the overall mean.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The ANOVA $F$ statistic becomes large when between-group variation is large relative to within-group error variation.
:::

---

## Total Variation and Decomposition {.compact .total-decomp}

:::: {.total-decomp-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 1.02fr 0.98fr; grid-template-rows: 205px 175px auto; gap: 16px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.defbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.66em; line-height: 1.17; padding: 17px 20px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Total variation</span>

Total variation measures how far all observations are from the overall mean.

$$
SSTotal=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(X_{ij}-\bar X)^2
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.66em; line-height: 1.17; padding: 17px 20px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">What ANOVA compares</span>

ANOVA compares variation **between group centers** to variation **inside the groups**.

$$
\text{between-group variation}
\qquad \text{vs.} \qquad
\text{within-group variation}
$$
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.66em; line-height: 1.17; padding: 17px 20px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Decomposition identity</span>

Total variation splits into treatment variation plus error variation:

$$
SSTotal=SSTr+SSE
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.17; padding: 17px 20px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Intuition</span>

If group means are close together, $SSTr$ is small.

If at least one group mean is far away, $SSTr$ becomes larger.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment style="grid-column: 1 / span 2; grid-row: 3; font-size: 0.66em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 14px 20px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Big picture</span>

ANOVA asks whether the **between-group variation** is large compared with the **within-group error variation**.
:::

::::

---

## The ANOVA Table {.compact .anova-table-slide}

:::: {.anova-table-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.52fr 0.48fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 16px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.54em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 15px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">ANOVA table structure</span>

| Source | df | SS | MS | $F^*$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Treatment | $k-1$ | $SSTr$ | $MSTr$ | $MSTr/MSE$ |
| Error | $n-k$ | $SSE$ | $MSE$ |  |
| Total | $n-1$ | $SSTotal$ |  |  |

<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 1.00em; margin-top: 10px;">

$$
SSTotal=SSTr+SSE
$$

$$
F^*=\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
$$

</div>

The p-value comes from the **right tail** of the \(F\) distribution.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 14px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Mean square rule</span>

A mean square is a sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom:

$$
MS=\frac{SS}{df}
$$

So in one-way ANOVA:

$$
MSTr=\frac{SSTr}{k-1},
\qquad
MSE=\frac{SSE}{n-k}
$$
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 14px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Degrees of freedom</span>

The degrees of freedom split the same way as the sums of squares:

$$
n-1=(k-1)+(n-k)
$$

Treatment variation uses \(k-1\) df, and error variation uses \(n-k\) df.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 14px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Test statistic and p-value</span>

The ANOVA test statistic is

$$
F^*=\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
$$

Under $H_0$,

$$
F^*\sim F_{k-1,\;n-k}
$$

The p-value is the right-tail area.
:::

::::

---

## ANOVA Hypothesis Test {.compact .anova-hyp-test}

:::: {.anova-test-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 16px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.defbox style="font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 16px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>

The null hypothesis says all population means are equal:

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
$$

The alternative says at least one population mean differs:

$$
H_a:\text{not all }\mu_i\text{ are equal}
$$
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 16px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>

Under $H_0$, the test statistic follows an $F$ distribution:

$$
F^* \sim F_{k-1,\;n-k}
$$

Numerator df:

$$
k-1
$$

Denominator df:

$$
n-k
$$
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 16px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Test statistic</span>

The ANOVA test statistic is

$$
F^*
=
\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
=
\frac{SSTr/(k-1)}{SSE/(n-k)}
$$

It compares between-group variation to within-group error variation.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 16px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">P-value</span>

The ANOVA p-value is the area to the **right** of $F^*$.

$$
p\text{-value}=P(F_{k-1,\;n-k}\ge F^*)
$$

Large $F^*$ values give evidence that the group means differ more than expected from random error alone.
:::

::::

---

## Assumptions of ANOVA {.compact .anova-assumptions}

:::: {.assumptions-flow style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 14px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.stat-card style="font-size: 0.66em; line-height: 1.22; padding: 18px 22px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Assumptions</span>

::: {.fragment}
- Observations are independent.
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Error terms, or residuals, are Normal.
:::

::: {.fragment}
- All groups have the same population variance:

$$
\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\cdots=\sigma_k^2=\sigma^2.
$$
:::
:::

::: {.defbox style="font-size: 0.66em; line-height: 1.20; padding: 17px 22px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Common variance estimate</span>

The common variance is estimated using the Mean Squared Error from ANOVA:

$$
\hat{\sigma}^2=MSE
$$
:::

::::

---

## ANOVA P-value Visual {.compact .anova-pvalue-visual}

:::: {.two-col-wide style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.46fr 0.54fr; gap: 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.66em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 16px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Right-tail reference distribution</span>

For $k=3$ groups and $n=18$ observations:

$$
df_1=k-1=2,
\qquad
df_2=n-k=15
$$

The shaded region is:

$$
P(F_{2,15}\ge F^*)
$$

In R, this is calculated with `lower.tail = FALSE`.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.60em; line-height: 1.12; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0; overflow: hidden;"}
<span class="label">Interactive right-tail area</span>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| out-width: "100%"

library(plotly)

df1 <- 2
df2 <- 15

p_levels <- c(0.10, 0.05, 0.01)
p_labels <- c("0.10", "0.05", "0.01")
F_values <- qf(1 - p_levels, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)

x_max <- 6.5
x <- seq(0.001, x_max, length.out = 700)
y <- df(x, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)

plot_df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

p <- plot_ly(width = 520, height = 300)

p <- p |>
  add_trace(
    data = plot_df,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "lines",
    line = list(color = "#263238", width = 3),
    hovertemplate = "F = %{x:.2f}<br>Density = %{y:.3f}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  )

for (i in seq_along(p_levels)) {
  F_star <- F_values[i]

  tail_x <- seq(F_star, x_max, length.out = 250)
  tail_y <- df(tail_x, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)

  shade_x <- c(F_star, tail_x, x_max)
  shade_y <- c(0, tail_y, 0)

  visible_now <- i == 2

  p <- p |>
    add_trace(
      x = shade_x,
      y = shade_y,
      type = "scatter",
      mode = "lines",
      fill = "toself",
      fillcolor = "rgba(245, 124, 0, 0.48)",
      line = list(color = "rgba(245, 124, 0, 0)", width = 0),
      hoverinfo = "skip",
      visible = visible_now,
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    add_trace(
      x = c(F_star, F_star),
      y = c(0, df(F_star, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)),
      type = "scatter",
      mode = "lines",
      line = list(color = "#00695c", width = 3, dash = "dash"),
      hovertemplate = paste0(
        "F* = ", round(F_star, 2),
        "<br>p-value = ", p_labels[i],
        "<extra></extra>"
      ),
      visible = visible_now,
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    add_trace(
      x = min(F_star + 0.45, x_max - 1.0),
      y = max(y) * 0.46,
      type = "scatter",
      mode = "text",
      text = paste0("p-value = ", p_labels[i]),
      textfont = list(color = "#263238", size = 13),
      hoverinfo = "skip",
      visible = visible_now,
      showlegend = FALSE
    )
}

buttons <- lapply(seq_along(p_levels), function(i) {
  visible <- rep(FALSE, 1 + 3 * length(p_levels))
  visible[1] <- TRUE

  start <- 2 + 3 * (i - 1)
  visible[start:(start + 2)] <- TRUE

  list(
    method = "update",
    label = paste0("p-value = ", p_labels[i]),
    args = list(
      list(visible = visible),
      list(
        title = paste0(
          "Right-tail area: P(F<sub>2,15</sub> ≥ ",
          round(F_values[i], 2),
          ") = ",
          p_labels[i]
        )
      )
    )
  )
})

p |>
  layout(
    title = paste0(
      "Right-tail area: P(F<sub>2,15</sub> ≥ ",
      round(F_values[2], 2),
      ") = ",
      p_labels[2]
    ),
    xaxis = list(
      title = "F",
      range = c(0, x_max),
      zeroline = FALSE,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Density",
      range = c(0, max(y) * 1.05),
      zeroline = FALSE,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
    ),
    margin = list(l = 45, r = 12, t = 54, b = 42),
    paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    plot_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    updatemenus = list(
      list(
        type = "dropdown",
        direction = "down",
        active = 1,
        x = 0.02,
        y = 1.14,
        xanchor = "left",
        yanchor = "top",
        buttons = buttons
      )
    )
  ) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = FALSE)
```
:::

::::

## Example: Campus Café Pickup Systems {.compact .cafe-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.42fr 0.58fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 14px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1 / span 2; font-size: 0.60em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 17px 19px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Problem</span>

A campus café wants to compare **three pickup systems** used during the same lunch rush period:

- mobile order,
- kiosk order,
- counter order.

For each system, the café records the number of minutes from **order confirmation** to **pickup**.

We want to know whether the population mean **pickup time** is the same for all three systems.

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3
$$

$$
H_a:\text{ at least one mean pickup time differs}
$$

Use a **one-way ANOVA at the 5% level**.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.50em; line-height: 1.06; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Observed data</span>

| Mobile order | Kiosk order | Counter order |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 5.0 | 6.5 | 7.8 |
| 6.0 | 6.5 | 8.8 |
| 7.0 | 8.5 | 9.8 |
| 7.0 | 9.5 | 10.6 |
| 8.0 | 9.5 | 11.8 |
| 9.0 | 10.5 | 12.4 |
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 17px 19px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">ANOVA setup</span>

The explanatory variable is the **pickup system**.

The response variable is **pickup wait time**.

There are $k=3$ groups and $n=18$ observations.

Each system has $n_i=6$ wait-time measurements.
:::

::::

---

## Campus Café: ANOVA Result {.cafe-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.60fr 0.40fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 16px 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.54em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 15px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;" data-fragment-index="1"}
<span class="label">Calculation table</span>

The grand mean is $\bar{x}=8.57$. The final two columns give the pieces that add to $SSE$ and $SSTr$.

| System | $n_i$ | $\bar{x}_i$ | $s_i^2$ | $(n_i-1)s_i^2$ | $n_i(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x})^2$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Mobile | 6 | 7.00 | 2.00 | 10.00 | 14.73 |
| Kiosk | 6 | 8.50 | 2.80 | 14.00 | 0.03 |
| Counter | 6 | 10.20 | 3.09 | 15.44 | 16.01 |
| **Totals** | **18** |  |  | **39.44** | **30.76** |

<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 1.08em; margin-top: 12px;">

$$
SSE=39.44,
\qquad
SSTr=30.76,
\qquad
SSTotal=70.20
$$

</div>
:::

::: {.notebox .calc-left .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1 / span 2; font-size: 0.56em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 15px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;" data-fragment-index="2"}
<span class="label">ANOVA table</span>

| Source | df | SS | MS | F | p-value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Treatment | 2 | 30.76 | 15.38 | 5.85 | 0.0132 |
| Error | 15 | 39.44 | 2.63 |  |  |
| Total | 17 | 70.20 |  |  |  |

$$
MSTr=\frac{30.76}{2}=15.38
$$

$$
MSE=\frac{39.44}{15}=2.63
$$

$$
F^*=\frac{15.38}{2.63}=5.85
$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.67em; line-height: 1.21; padding: 17px 19px; margin-bottom: 0;" data-fragment-index="3"}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>

Since $p=0.0132<0.05$, reject $H_0$.

There is evidence that **not all pickup systems** have the same population mean pickup wait time.

The ANOVA test tells us that at least one system has a different mean. It does **not** tell us which systems differ.
:::

::::

---

## Visual: Campus Café Pickup Systems

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

cafe <- data.frame(
  wait_time = c(5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0,
                6.5, 6.5, 8.5, 9.5, 9.5, 10.5,
                7.8, 8.8, 9.8, 10.6, 11.8, 12.4),
  system = factor(
    rep(c("Mobile order", "Kiosk order", "Counter order"), each = 6),
    levels = c("Mobile order", "Kiosk order", "Counter order")
  )
)

cafe_ci <- cafe |>
  group_by(system) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_wait = mean(wait_time),
    sd_wait = sd(wait_time),
    se = sd_wait / sqrt(n),
    t_star = qt(0.975, df = n - 1),
    lower = mean_wait - t_star * se,
    upper = mean_wait + t_star * se,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

plot_ly(
  cafe_ci,
  x = ~system,
  y = ~mean_wait,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers",
  marker = list(
    size = 12,
    color = plot_cols$red,
    line = list(color = "white", width = 1.4)
  ),
  error_y = list(
    type = "data",
    array = ~upper - mean_wait,
    arrayminus = ~mean_wait - lower,
    color = "rgba(0,105,92,0.75)",
    thickness = 2.3,
    width = 8
  ),
  hovertemplate = paste(
    "System: %{x}",
    "<br>Mean wait time: %{y:.2f}",
    "<br>95% CI: (%{customdata[0]:.2f}, %{customdata[1]:.2f})",
    "<extra></extra>"
  ),
  customdata = ~cbind(lower, upper),
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  plotly_anova_layout(
    title = "95% confidence intervals for mean pickup wait time by system",
    x_title = "Ordering system",
    y_title = "Mean wait time (minutes)",
    height = 390,
    margin = list(l = 76, r = 25, t = 60, b = 70)
  ) |>
  layout(
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Mean wait time (minutes)",
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.07)",
      tickmode = "linear",
      tick0 = 5,
      dtick = 1,
      range = c(4.8, 12.4)
    )
  )
```

::: {.thinkbox style="font-size: 0.68em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-top: 10px;"}
The **red dots** show the sample mean pickup wait time for each ordering system. The vertical bars show **95% confidence intervals for the group means**, matching the textbook-style visual.
:::

## Example: Short-Form Video Edit Styles {.video-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.43fr 0.57fr; gap: 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 17px 19px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Problem</span>

A creator wants to compare **four video edit styles** used on comparable short videos from the same account:

- clean cut,
- captions-first,
- meme overlay,
- story hook.

For each video, the creator records the **viewer watch time** in seconds.

We want to know whether the **population mean watch time** is the same for all four edit styles.

<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 0.95em; margin-top: 12px; margin-bottom: 12px;">

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=\mu_4
$$

$$
H_a:\text{at least one mean watch time differs}
$$

</div>

Use a **one-way ANOVA at the 5% level**.
:::

::: {.col style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr; gap: 16px;"}

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.53em; line-height: 1.08; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Observed data</span>

| Clean cut | Captions-first | Meme overlay | Story hook |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 | 39 | 35 | 46 |
| 36 | 39 | 40 | 49 |
| 38 | 44 | 41 | 52 |
| 40 | 49 | 42 | 55 |
| 44 | 49 | 47 | 58 |
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment style="font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.22; padding: 17px 19px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">ANOVA setup</span>

The explanatory variable is the **edit style**.

The response variable is **viewer watch time**.

There are $k=4$ groups and $n=20$ observations.

Each edit style has $n_i=5$ watch-time measurements.
:::

:::

## Short-Form Video: ANOVA Result {.video-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.60fr 0.40fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 16px 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.52em; line-height: 1.09; padding: 15px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation table</span>

The grand mean is $\bar{x}=43.75$. The final two columns give the pieces that add to $SSE$ and $SSTr$.

| Edit style | $n_i$ | $\bar{x}_i$ | $s_i^2$ | $(n_i-1)s_i^2$ | $n_i(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x})^2$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Clean cut | 5 | 38.00 | 20.00 | 80.00 | 165.31 |
| Captions-first | 5 | 44.00 | 25.00 | 100.00 | 0.31 |
| Meme overlay | 5 | 41.00 | 18.50 | 74.00 | 37.81 |
| Story hook | 5 | 52.00 | 22.50 | 90.00 | 340.31 |
| **Totals** | **20** |  |  | **344.00** | **543.75** |

<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 1.08em; margin-top: 12px;">

$$
SSE=344.00,
\qquad
SSTr=543.75,
\qquad
SSTotal=887.75
$$

</div>
:::

::: {.notebox .calc-left .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1 / span 2; font-size: 0.56em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 15px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">ANOVA table</span>

| Source | df | SS | MS | F | p-value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Treatment | 3 | 543.75 | 181.25 | 8.43 | 0.0014 |
| Error | 16 | 344.00 | 21.50 |  |  |
| Total | 19 | 887.75 |  |  |  |

$$
MSTr=\frac{543.75}{3}=181.25
$$

$$
MSE=\frac{344.00}{16}=21.50
$$

$$
F^*=\frac{181.25}{21.50}=8.43
$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.67em; line-height: 1.21; padding: 17px 19px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>

Since $p=0.0014<0.05$, reject $H_0$.

There is evidence that **not all edit styles** have the same population mean viewer watch time.

The ANOVA test tells us that at least one edit style has a different mean. It does **not** tell us which styles differ.

```{r}
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Mean watch time (seconds)",

      showline = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.07)",
      tickmode = "linear",
      tick0 = 32,
      dtick = 4,
      range = c(30, 60)
    )
  )
```

## What If ANOVA Rejects? {.compact .anova-rejects}

:::: {.anova-flow style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto auto auto; gap: 13px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.defbox style="font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.17; padding: 14px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Global ANOVA result</span>

ANOVA tests whether all population means are equal:

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
\qquad \text{vs.} \qquad
H_a:\text{at least one mean is different}
$$
:::

:::: {.three-col style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; gap: 14px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Important limitation</span>

Rejecting $H_0$ tells us that **not all means are equal**.

It does **not** tell us which specific groups differ.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Follow-up question</span>

After a significant ANOVA result, we ask:

$$
\text{Which means are different?}
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment style="font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Pairwise comparisons</span>

For three groups:

$$
\mu_1-\mu_2,\qquad
\mu_1-\mu_3,\qquad
\mu_2-\mu_3
$$

With $k$ groups:

$$
m=\binom{k}{2}
$$
:::

::::

::: {.examplebox .fragment style="font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 13px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Next step</span>

Use pairwise confidence intervals to compare specific group means: first **Fisher's LSD**, then **Bonferroni**.
:::

::::

---

## Pairwise Confidence Intervals {.compact .pairwise-ci}

:::: {.pairwise-ci-flow style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr; gap: 14px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.defbox style="font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 13px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">General idea</span>

After ANOVA rejects, compare two population means using an interval for $\mu_i-\mu_j$:

<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 0.95em; margin-top: 6px; margin-bottom: 4px;">

$$
(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j)
\pm
t^*
\sqrt{
MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)
}
\qquad
\text{where } \hat{\sigma}^2=MSE
$$

</div>
:::

:::: {.three-col style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; gap: 14px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.59em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Fisher's LSD</span>

Use the ordinary two-sided critical value:

$$
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/2,\;n-k}
$$

This gives **narrower intervals**, so it has more power to detect differences.

It is less conservative when many pairs are compared.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.59em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Bonferroni</span>

First count the number of pairwise comparisons:

$$
m=\binom{k}{2}
$$

Then use the adjusted critical value:

$$
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/(2m),\;n-k}
$$

This gives **wider intervals**.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.59em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Decision rule</span>

A pair is declared **different** when the interval for $\mu_i-\mu_j$ does **not contain 0**.

If the interval contains 0, the pair is **not clearly different**.

So the whole method is:

$$
\text{interval avoids }0
\Rightarrow
\text{different}
$$
:::

::::

::::

---

## Fisher's LSD: The Idea {.compact .fisher-idea}

:::: {.fisher-flow style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto auto auto; gap: 13px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.defbox style="font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.17; padding: 14px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Least Significant Difference</span>

Fisher's LSD compares two group means after the overall ANOVA test has rejected $H_0$.

For a pair of groups $i$ and $j$, we compare the observed mean difference:

$$
\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j
$$
:::

:::: {.three-col style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; gap: 14px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Shared error estimate</span>

Use the pooled within-group variation from ANOVA:

$$
MSE
$$

This estimates the common variance $\sigma^2$.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Ordinary t critical value</span>

Fisher's LSD uses:

$$
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/2,\;n-k}
$$

The degrees of freedom come from the ANOVA error row.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">LSD cutoff</span>

When group sizes are $n_i$ and $n_j$:

$$
LSD=
t^*
\sqrt{
MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)
}
$$
:::

::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 13px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">How to decide</span>

If

$$
|\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j|>LSD,
$$

then the pair is declared **different**. Fisher's LSD is powerful, but it is less conservative when many pairwise comparisons are made.
:::

::::

----

## Example: Badminton Drills — Fisher's LSD {.compact .badminton-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.40fr 0.60fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 13px 16px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.55em; line-height: 1.09; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Problem</span>

A badminton coach compares three drill programs for improving **serve-target accuracy**.

After two months, each player completes the same accuracy test out of 40.

| Static targets | Footwork + serve | Coach-fed targets |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 19 | 24 | 26 |
| 20 | 25 | 27 |
| 21 | 26 | 28 |
| 23 | 28 | 29 |
| 24 | 29 | 30 |
| 25 | 30 | 31 |

ANOVA rejects $H_0$. Which drill programs differ using **Fisher's LSD**?
:::

::: {.notebox .calc-left .fragment style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.55em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Setup from ANOVA</span>

$$
MSE=4.90,
\qquad
v=n-k=18-3=15
$$

$$
\bar{x}_1=22,
\qquad
\bar{x}_2=27,
\qquad
\bar{x}_3=28.5
$$

Each group has $n_i=6$.
:::

::: {.stat-card .calc-left .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1 / span 2; font-size: 0.57em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 15px 17px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; flex-direction: column;"}
<span class="label">Fisher LSD calculation</span>

::: {.fragment}
Use the ordinary critical value:

$$
t^*=t_{0.975,15}=2.131
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Because all groups have size 6, the standard error is the same for every pair:

$$
SE=
\sqrt{
4.90
\left(
\frac16+\frac16
\right)
}
=
1.28
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
The least significant difference is

$$
LSD=2.131(1.28)=2.72
$$

So each pairwise interval is:

$$
(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j)\pm 2.72
$$
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top: auto;"}
<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 1.10em; line-height: 1.14; padding-top: 12px;">

<span class="label" style="font-size: 1.02em; margin-bottom: 4px;">Pairwise Fisher LSD intervals</span>

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Static} - \text{Footwork}
&:\ -5.00\pm2.72=(-7.72,\,-2.28)\\[7pt]
\text{Static} - \text{Coach-fed}
&:\ -6.50\pm2.72=(-9.22,\,-3.78)\\[7pt]
\text{Footwork} - \text{Coach-fed}
&:\ -1.50\pm2.72=(-4.22,\,1.22)
\end{aligned}
$$

</div>
:::

:::

::::

## Example: Phone Case Drop-Test Costs — Fisher's LSD {.compact .phone-case-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.40fr 0.60fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 13px 16px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.51em; line-height: 1.06; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Problem</span>

A device lab compares four phone case designs after a standardized drop test.

For each case design, the lab records the **repair cost** after impact.

| Clear | Slim | Wallet | Rugged |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 69 | 73 | 78 | 85 |
| 71 | 75 | 80 | 87 |
| 73 | 77 | 82 | 89 |
| 75 | 79 | 84 | 91 |
| 75 | 79 | 84 | 91 |
| 77 | 81 | 86 | 93 |
| 79 | 83 | 88 | 95 |
| 81 | 85 | 90 | 97 |

ANOVA rejects $H_0$. Which case designs differ using **Fisher's LSD**?
:::

::: {.notebox .calc-left .fragment style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.55em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Setup from ANOVA</span>

$$
MSE=16.00,
\qquad
v=n-k=32-4=28
$$

$$
\bar{x}_{Clear}=75,\quad
\bar{x}_{Slim}=79,\quad
\bar{x}_{Wallet}=84,\quad
\bar{x}_{Rugged}=91
$$

Each group has $n_i=8$.
:::

::: {.stat-card .calc-left .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1 / span 2; font-size: 0.55em; line-height: 1.08; padding: 15px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Fisher LSD calculation</span>

::: {.fragment}
Use the ordinary critical value:

$$
t^*=t_{0.975,28}=2.048
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Because all groups have size 8, the standard error is the same for every pair:

$$
SE=
\sqrt{
16.00
\left(
\frac18+\frac18
\right)
}
=
2.00
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
The least significant difference is

$$
LSD=2.048(2.00)=4.10
$$

So each pairwise interval is:

$$
(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j)\pm 4.10
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 1.02em; line-height: 1.10; margin-top: 10px;">

<span class="label" style="font-size: 1.02em; margin-bottom: 4px;">Pairwise Fisher LSD intervals</span>

:::: {.two-col style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 10px; align-items: start;"}

::: {}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Clear} - \text{Slim}
&:\ -4.00\pm4.10=(-8.10,\,0.10)\\[5pt]
\text{Clear} - \text{Wallet}
&:\ -9.00\pm4.10=(-13.10,\,-4.90)\\[5pt]
\text{Clear} - \text{Rugged}
&:\ -16.00\pm4.10=(-20.10,\,-11.90)
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Slim} - \text{Wallet}
&:\ -5.00\pm4.10=(-9.10,\,-0.90)\\[5pt]
\text{Slim} - \text{Rugged}
&:\ -12.00\pm4.10=(-16.10,\,-7.90)\\[5pt]
\text{Wallet} - \text{Rugged}
&:\ -7.00\pm4.10=(-11.10,\,-2.90)
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::::

</div>
:::

:::

## Visual: Badminton Drill Accuracy Scores

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

badminton <- data.frame(
  score = c(19, 20, 21, 23, 24, 25,
            24, 25, 26, 28, 29, 30,
            26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31),
  drill = factor(
    rep(c("Static targets", "Footwork + serve", "Coach-fed targets"), each = 6),
    levels = c("Static targets", "Footwork + serve", "Coach-fed targets")
  )
)

badminton_ci <- badminton |>
  group_by(drill) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_score = mean(score),
    sd_score = sd(score),
    se = sd_score / sqrt(n),
    t_star = qt(0.975, df = n - 1),
    lower = mean_score - t_star * se,
    upper = mean_score + t_star * se,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

plot_ly(
  badminton_ci,
  x = ~drill,
  y = ~mean_score,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers",
  marker = list(
    size = 12,
    color = plot_cols$red,
    line = list(color = "white", width = 1.4)
  ),
  error_y = list(
    type = "data",
    array = ~upper - mean_score,
    arrayminus = ~mean_score - lower,
    color = "rgba(0,105,92,0.75)",
    thickness = 2.3,
    width = 8
  ),
  hovertemplate = paste(
    "Drill: %{x}",
    "<br>Mean score: %{y:.2f}",
    "<br>95% CI: (%{customdata[0]:.2f}, %{customdata[1]:.2f})",
    "<extra></extra>"
  ),
  customdata = ~cbind(lower, upper),
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  plotly_anova_layout(
    title = "95% confidence intervals for mean accuracy score by drill program",
    x_title = "Badminton drill program",
    y_title = "Mean accuracy score",
    height = 390,
    margin = list(l = 76, r = 25, t = 60, b = 78)
  ) |>
  layout(
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Mean accuracy score",
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.07)",
      tickmode = "linear",
      tick0 = 20,
      dtick = 2,
      range = c(18, 32)
    )
  )
```

::: {.thinkbox style="font-size: 0.68em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-top: 10px;"}
The **red dots** show the sample mean accuracy score for each drill program. The vertical bars show **95% confidence intervals for the group means**, matching the textbook-style visual.
:::

A pair is declared **different** when the interval does **not contain 0**.

:::

```{r}
    "Case design: %{x}",
    "<br>Mean repair cost: %{y:.2f}",
    "<br>95% CI: (%{customdata[0]:.2f}, %{customdata[1]:.2f})",
    "<extra></extra>"
  ),
  customdata = ~cbind(lower, upper),
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  plotly_anova_layout(
    title = "95% confidence intervals for mean repair cost by phone case design",
    x_title = "Phone case design",
    y_title = "Mean repair cost",
    height = 390,
    margin = list(l = 76, r = 25, t = 60, b = 70)
  ) |>
  layout(
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Mean repair cost",
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.07)",
      tickmode = "linear",
      tick0 = 70,
      dtick = 5,
      range = c(68, 96)
    )
  )
```

::: {.thinkbox style="font-size: 0.68em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-top: 10px;"}
The **red dots** show the sample mean repair cost for each phone case design. The vertical bars show **95% confidence intervals for the group means**, matching the textbook-style visual.
:::

## Bonferroni: Why Adjust? {.compact .bonferroni-idea}

:::: {.bonferroni-flow style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto auto auto; gap: 13px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.defbox style="font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 13px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">The issue</span>

After ANOVA rejects, we may compare many pairs of means.

Each pairwise comparison has a chance of making a Type I error, so doing many comparisons increases the chance of making **at least one false discovery**.
:::

:::: {.three-col style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; gap: 14px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">1. Count comparisons</span>

With $k$ groups, the number of pairwise comparisons is

$$
m=\binom{k}{2}.
$$

For example, if $k=4$,

$$
m=\binom{4}{2}=6.
$$
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">2. Experiment-wise error</span>

If each comparison uses error rate $\alpha$, then the chance of making at least one Type I error is

$$
\alpha_E=1-(1-\alpha)^m.
$$

As $m$ increases, $\alpha_E$ increases.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">3. Bonferroni correction</span>

To keep the overall error rate controlled, Bonferroni uses a smaller per-comparison level:

$$
\frac{\alpha}{m}.
$$

For a two-sided interval, this gives

$$
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/(2m),\;n-k}.
$$
:::

::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.17; padding: 13px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Key idea</span>

**Fisher's LSD** is more powerful, but it does not control the experiment-wise Type I error rate.

**Bonferroni** is more cautious: it uses wider intervals to protect against making false discoveries across many pairwise comparisons.
:::

::::

## Example: Phone Case Drop-Test Costs — Bonferroni {.compact .phone-case-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.40fr 0.60fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 13px 16px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.51em; line-height: 1.06; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Problem</span>

A device lab compares four phone case designs after a standardized drop test.

For each case design, the lab records the **repair cost** after impact.

| Clear | Slim | Wallet | Rugged |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 69 | 73 | 78 | 85 |
| 71 | 75 | 80 | 87 |
| 73 | 77 | 82 | 89 |
| 75 | 79 | 84 | 91 |
| 75 | 79 | 84 | 91 |
| 77 | 81 | 86 | 93 |
| 79 | 83 | 88 | 95 |
| 81 | 85 | 90 | 97 |

ANOVA rejects $H_0$. Which case designs differ using **Bonferroni**?
:::

::: {.notebox .calc-left .fragment style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.54em; line-height: 1.09; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Setup from ANOVA</span>

$$
MSE=16.00,
\qquad
v=n-k=32-4=28
$$

$$
\bar{x}_{Clear}=75,\quad
\bar{x}_{Slim}=79,\quad
\bar{x}_{Wallet}=84,\quad
\bar{x}_{Rugged}=91
$$

There are

$$
m=\binom{4}{2}=6
$$

pairwise comparisons.
:::

::: {.stat-card .calc-left .fragment style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1 / span 2; font-size: 0.54em; line-height: 1.07; padding: 15px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Bonferroni calculation</span>

Use the Bonferroni critical value:

$$
t^*
=
t_{1-\alpha/(2m),\,28}
=
t_{1-0.05/(2\cdot6),\,28}
=
t_{0.99583,\,28}
=
2.84
$$

::: {.fragment}
Because all groups have size 8, the standard error is still

$$
SE=
\sqrt{
16.00
\left(
\frac18+\frac18
\right)
}
=
2.00
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
The Bonferroni margin of error is

$$
ME=2.84(2.00)=5.68
$$

So each pairwise interval is:

$$
(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j)\pm 5.68
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 1.00em; line-height: 1.08; margin-top: 22px;">

<span class="label" style="font-size: 1.02em; margin-bottom: 4px;">Pairwise Bonferroni intervals</span>

:::: {.two-col style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 10px; align-items: start;"}

::: {}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Clear} - \text{Slim}
&:\ -4.00\pm5.68=(-9.68,\,1.68)\\[5pt]
\text{Clear} - \text{Wallet}
&:\ -9.00\pm5.68=(-14.68,\,-3.32)\\[5pt]
\text{Clear} - \text{Rugged}
&:\ -16.00\pm5.68=(-21.68,\,-10.32)
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Slim} - \text{Wallet}
&:\ -5.00\pm5.68=(-10.68,\,0.68)\\[5pt]
\text{Slim} - \text{Rugged}
&:\ -12.00\pm5.68=(-17.68,\,-6.32)\\[5pt]
\text{Wallet} - \text{Rugged}
&:\ -7.00\pm5.68=(-12.68,\,-1.32)
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::::

</div>
:::

:::

::::

## Phone Case Drop-Test Costs — Bonferroni Results {.compact .phone-case-results}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.40fr 0.60fr; gap: 16px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.taskbox style="font-size: 0.51em; line-height: 1.06; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Problem</span>

A device lab compares four phone case designs after a standardized drop test.

For each case design, the lab records the **repair cost** after impact.

| Clear | Slim | Wallet | Rugged |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 69 | 73 | 78 | 85 |
| 71 | 75 | 80 | 87 |
| 73 | 77 | 82 | 89 |
| 75 | 79 | 84 | 91 |
| 75 | 79 | 84 | 91 |
| 77 | 81 | 86 | 93 |
| 79 | 83 | 88 | 95 |
| 81 | 85 | 90 | 97 |

ANOVA rejects $H_0$. Which case designs differ using **Bonferroni**?
:::

::: {.col style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto auto auto; gap: 12px;"}

::: {.stat-card .calc-left style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.12; padding: 14px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Read the Bonferroni intervals</span>

A pair is declared **different** when the interval does **not contain 0**.

$$
\text{interval avoids }0
\Rightarrow
\text{different}
\qquad
\text{interval contains }0
\Rightarrow
\text{not clearly different}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.43fr 0.57fr; gap: 12px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.notebox .fragment style="font-size: 0.52em; line-height: 1.09; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Intervals that contain 0</span>

$$
\text{Clear}-\text{Slim}
$$

$$
(-9.68,\;1.68)
$$

$$
\text{Slim}-\text{Wallet}
$$

$$
(-10.68,\;0.68)
$$

These pairs are **not clearly different**.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment style="font-size: 0.50em; line-height: 1.08; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Intervals that avoid 0</span>

| Pair | Bonferroni interval | Decision |
|---|---:|---|
| Clear - Wallet | $(-14.68,\,-3.32)$ | Different |
| Clear - Rugged | $(-21.68,\,-10.32)$ | Different |
| Slim - Rugged | $(-17.68,\,-6.32)$ | Different |
| Wallet - Rugged | $(-12.68,\,-1.32)$ | Different |
:::

::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 13px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Answer</span>

Using Bonferroni, **Clear** and **Slim** are not clearly different, and **Slim** and **Wallet** are not clearly different.

However, **Rugged** is clearly higher than all other case designs.
:::

:::

## Check in R: Pairwise Comparisons {.compact-r}

:::: {.two-col-wide style="grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Badminton drill example</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

library(DescTools)

score <- c(19, 20, 21, 23, 24, 25,
           24, 25, 26, 28, 29, 30,
           26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31)

drill <- factor(rep(c("Static", "Footwork", "Coach-fed"), each = 6))

fit <- aov(score ~ drill)

PostHocTest(fit, method = "lsd")

PostHocTest(fit, method = "bonferroni")
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}

```{webr}

          85, 87, 89, 91, 91, 93, 95, 97)
```

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A one-way ANOVA with $k=4$ groups has a significant p-value. How many pairwise mean comparisons are possible?
::::

- 3
- [6]{.correct data-explanation="The number of pairwise comparisons is choose(k, 2). With k = 4, choose(4, 2) = 6."}
- 8
- 16

## Final Checklist

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Before calculating ANOVA</span>

- Identify the response variable.
- Identify the grouping variable.
- State $H_0:\mu_1=\cdots=\mu_k$.
- Check independence, Normal errors, and equal variance.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">After calculating ANOVA</span>

- Fill in df, SS, MS, and $F^*$.
- Use the right-tail F p-value.
- Reject only when the p-value is small.
- If ANOVA rejects, use pairwise comparisons.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One slide takeaway.** ANOVA compares several means by asking whether between-group variation is large compared with within-group error variation.
:::
